title: Dicts and sets
short: Look things up by key in one step, and drop duplicates.
what: A dict maps keys to values: count["cat"] = 2. A set is a bag of unique keys with no values. Both answer "is this here?" in one step instead of scanning.
analogy: A dict is a phone book: name to number. A set is a guest list: you only care whether a name is on it, and nobody is listed twice.

frames.label: count = {}
frames.say: count = {} is an empty dict. We will count the words in ["cat", "dog", "cat"].

frames.label: count[w] = count.get(w, 0) + 1
frames.say: "cat" is not a key yet, so count.get("cat", 0) returns 0. Add 1 and store it under "cat".

frames.label: count[w] = count.get(w, 0) + 1
frames.say: "dog" is new too, so it also starts at 1.

frames.label: count[w] = count.get(w, 0) + 1
frames.say: "cat" again: get finds 1, so it becomes 2. "cat" in count is True, found in one step.

frames.label: groups.setdefault(len(w), []).append(w)
frames.say: setdefault(k, []) returns the list under k, creating an empty one first if needed. Then append to it.

frames.label: a = {1, 2, 3}; b = {2, 3, 4}
frames.say: A set keeps unique items, no values. a = {1, 2, 3}, b = {2, 3, 4}. a.add(3) changes nothing: 3 is already in.

frames.label: a & b
frames.say: a & b keeps what is in both. a | b keeps everything in either.

frames.label: a - b
frames.say: a - b keeps what only a has. b.remove(4) takes 4 out; it raises KeyError if 4 is missing, discard does not.

when: Count how many times each thing appears
Group items that share a key
What do two lists have in common?
watch: d[k] on a missing key raises KeyError. Use d.get(k, 0), or a defaultdict.
{} is an empty dict, not a set. An empty set is set().
A list cannot be a key or a set item. Turn it into a tuple first.
